questions.q: Why is CPU utilization a poor autoscaling signal for GPU inference services?
options: CPU utilization cannot be measured in Kubernetes
The CPU sits mostly idle while the GPU does the real work, so CPU% barely reflects actual load
CPU utilization is only available for batch jobs, not real-time serving
Kubernetes does not support scaling on any custom metric
questions.explain: An inference pod's bottleneck is GPU compute, not CPU. CPU utilization can stay low even when the service is fully saturated and queuing requests.

questions.q: What does KEDA add on top of Kubernetes' standard Horizontal Pod Autoscaler?
options: The ability to run pods without containers
Support for external metric sources, like a Prometheus query or queue length, for event-driven scaling
A replacement for GPUs entirely
Automatic model quantization during scaling
questions.explain: KEDA extends the standard autoscaler with external metrics such as a Prometheus query or message-queue length — exactly what signals like queue depth require.

questions.q: Why does pure reactive autoscaling always lag behind a traffic spike for GPU inference?
options: Reactive autoscaling checks metrics only once per day
Kubernetes pods cannot be added faster than one per hour
A new replica isn't useful until it finishes loading model weights onto the GPU, which can take seconds to minutes
GPUs cannot run more than one replica at a time
questions.explain: Cold start — loading weights and initializing the framework — takes real time, so a replica created in response to a spike isn't actually serving traffic until that finishes.

questions.q: Which strategy directly addresses the cold-start gap in GPU autoscaling?
options: Setting minReplicaCount to zero so no GPU is ever idle
Keeping a warm minimum of already-loaded replicas, or scaling ahead of a known traffic pattern on a schedule
Disabling the autoscaler entirely
Only ever running one replica regardless of load
questions.explain: Keeping warm, already-loaded replicas and scaling ahead of predictable peaks both provide ready capacity before demand actually arrives, bypassing the cold-start delay.

questions.q: What should happen to a replica that an autoscaler decides to remove?
options: It should be killed immediately regardless of in-flight requests
It should stop receiving new requests, finish in-flight ones, then terminate after a grace period
It should be converted into a backup database
It should be left running forever to avoid any risk
questions.explain: A safe scale-down drains the replica — no new requests, finish existing ones — before terminating it, respecting a grace period and a sensible minimum replica floor.
